abstract: ABSTRACT Enzalutamide and abiraterone are hormonal treatments that improve survival in metastatic castration‐resistant prostate cancer. Identifying genetic variants associated with the clearance of these drugs may aid in improved dosing and outcomes. We performed genetic association studies of enzalutamide and abiraterone oral clearance in the Alliance A031201 clinical trial. Genome‐wide genotyping was performed with the primary analysis limited to European‐descent participants. Pharmacogene metabolic phenotypes were estimated using PyPGx and Stargazer. Associations of metabolic activity groups for CYP3A4 , CYP3A5 , CYP2C19 and SLCO1B1 with enzalutamide clearance ( N = 706) and CYP3A4 , SLCO2B1 and UGT1A4 with abiraterone clearance ( N = 323) were tested by linear regression. Targeted SNP associations were assessed for abiraterone clearance at loci proximal to major metabolizing genes. Full genome‐wide association studies were performed for both sets of clearance values. No significant associations were identified between metabolic phenotypes and enzalutamide or abiraterone oral clearance SNPs in the SULT2A1 5′ flanking region were significantly associated with lower abiraterone clearance, (rs296373, minor allele frequency = 0.15, β = −0.457, p = 3.2E‐06). Liver protein and liver and adrenal gland gene expression QTL databases indicated significantly lower SULT2A1 expression patterns for individuals carrying associated alleles, likely explaining the lower abiraterone oral clearance. CYP2C8*3 was associated with higher enzalutamide clearance ( p = 0.012), but this was not significant after correction for multiple testing. This study is the first to identify the genetic association of SULT2A1, known to be involved in the metabolism of steroids in the liver and adrenal glands, with abiraterone clearance. Genetic variation in SULT2A1 may be useful to inform personalized dosing of abiraterone. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01949337

Methods
2.1
Patient Population
Details regarding the overall trial eligibility criteria and participant characteristics are described elsewhere [
1
]. Briefly, patients were enrolled in Alliance A031201 in a 1:1 ratio to receive either enzalutamide monotherapy (160 mg once daily by mouth) or enzalutamide plus AAP (abiraterone 1000 mg once daily and prednisone 5 mg twice daily by mouth). A total of 1311 men with untreated mCRPC were randomly assigned: 657 to enzalutamide and 654 to enzalutamide plus AAP. Clinical and demographic characteristics considered in our study included age (years), body mass index (BMI; kg/m
2
), body surface area (BSA) estimated via the Mosteller equation, and self‐reported race.
2.2
Pharmacokinetic Analyses
For patients receiving enzalutamide alone or enzalutamide plus abiraterone, 4‐mL venous blood samples for abiraterone/enzalutamide concentrations were obtained in EDTA tubes at baseline, and at each scheduled monthly follow‐up clinic visit for up to six cycles while still receiving study drug therapy. Time of day was obtained and documented for each blood sample. At these follow‐up visits, a patient pharmacokinetic questionnaire was requested for information about the prior 48‐h dosing of abiraterone/enzalutamide, detailing the time of day the last two doses of the study drug were taken, and when the doses were taken in relation to meals.
On collection, samples were mixed immediately by gently inverting the tube at least 8–10 times to ensure thorough mixing of the anticoagulant, then placed on ice for less than 30 min during the sampling period. Samples were centrifuged at 4°C at 2000
g
× for 10 min to separate plasma from red cells. Plasma (1 mL) was aliquoted into 1.8‐mL cryovials labeled with patient ID, date of the sample, and the time of sample acquisition. Sample timing was indicated as the actual time the sample was obtained. Sample handling from collection to storage did not exceed 60 min.
Processed patient plasma aliquots were stored at −20°C or below and shipped to the Alliance Pharmacology/Pharmacokinetic core lab at the University of Pittsburgh where they were analyzed in batches (by JHB) for concentrations of enzalutamide and abiraterone using a published liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS–MS) assay [
13
]. The plasma concentrations of enzalutamide and abiraterone were analyzed by nonlinear mixed‐effect modeling using Pumas AI [
14
] to estimate population apparent oral clearance of each drug for each participant. Clearance was used as the primary endpoint in this analysis as it is most directly related to the CYP‐mediated metabolic elimination of the drug.
2.3
Genome‐Wide Genotyping
All patients enrolled in Alliance A031201 were given the option to consent for germline DNA analysis, which involved collection of a single blood sample (10 mL in a lavender top tube) at baseline (or any follow‐up visit). For patients who consented, germline DNA was extracted from peripheral blood mononuclear cells using the Promega Maxwell blood DNA kit. DNA samples were stored at the Alliance Biorepository at Ohio State University (OSU), then shipped to the Laboratory for Pharmacogenomics at the Riken Institute in Yokohama, Japan where the genotyping was performed.
Genome‐wide germline genotyping was performed on DNA samples with the InfiniumOmniExpressExome‐8v1‐4_A1 array as per the manufacturer's instructions. Sixteen duplicate pairs of participants and two CEPH trios were included in the genotyping for QC purposes. Individual SNPs were excluded for quality control (QC) based on low call rate (< 98%). Sample‐level QC exclusions included low call rate (< 98%), sex discordance with reported sex, and low chromosomal heterozygosity. Relatedness among participants was assessed using KING Robust [
15
]. Genetic ancestry was assessed with ADMIXTURE [
16
] using study samples along with reference population samples from the 1000 genomes Phase III AFR, AMR, EAS, EUR, and SAS super‐populations. Participants were determined to be of primarily European ancestry based on an ADMIXTURE EUR estimate > 0.80, and leading principal components (PCs) were derived based on directly genotyped SNPs on the EUR subset.
Genotype imputation was performed on all QC‐passed samples using the TOPMed Imputation Server [
17
] under default settings. Post‐imputation QC included removal of imputed variants with an imputation
R
2
< 0.8 or minor allele frequency (MAF) < 0.01. All reported genomic positions are based on build GRCh38.
2.4
Pharmacogene Selection
Genes encoding enzymes and transporters involved in the metabolism of enzalutamide and abiraterone were pre‐specified for analysis based on pathways in PharmGKB and current literature (Figure
S1
). Where possible, we utilized the genome‐wide genotyping results to determine star allele metabolic activity (Table
S1
).
CYP3A4
, the primary metabolic enzyme for enzalutamide [
18
,
19
] was pre‐specified for the primary metabolizer phenotype analysis for enzalutamide clearance with
CYP2C8
,
CYP3A5
,
CYP2C19
and
SLCO1B1
as secondary analyses. For abiraterone analysis, metabolic activity could not be assessed for
SULT2A1
(the major metabolizer of abiraterone),
HSD3B1
, and
HSD3B2
(which metabolize abiraterone to delta 4 abiraterone), and association analyses were limited to the single SNP approach.
CYP3A4
,
SLCO2B1
and
UGT1A4
were analyzed for both metabolic phenotypes and single‐SNP associations.
2.5
Candidate Gene Phenotyping
CYP3A4
,
CYP3A5
,
CYP2C8
,
CYP2C19
,
SLCO1B1
,
SLCO2B1
and
UGT1A4
are among the 87 pharmacogenes supported by the PGx software PyPGx [
20
]. Star allele genotypes and corresponding metabolizer phenotypes for these six genes were predicted by PyPGx for all participants using the imputed genotyping data. Quantitative allele activity scores for the predicted star allele genotypes were additionally assigned using databases from Stargazer [
21
,
22
]. Overall pharmacogene activity values at the participant level were scored additively, such that “normal” (wild type) functional alleles were assigned a value of 1, alleles that respectively reflected decreased or increased activity were given lower/higher activity scores, and total activity per participant was the sum of the two allele activity scores.
2.6
Statistical Analyses
Continuous variables were summarized by mean and standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile range (IQR), while nominal variables were summarized by counts and percentages. Association testing between pharmacogene activity and estimated clearance values was performed using linear regression. Regression analyses were performed unadjusted as well as adjusted for potential strong explanatory variables and confounders, as selected from age, BMI, BSA, treatment arm (enzalutamide only), and leading genetic PCs. Variance stabilizing transformations (e.g., log) were considered for clearance values, as appropriate, while linearity assumptions for covariates were assessed and polynomial terms were added as necessary. Sensitivity analyses included modeling metabolizer phenotypes categorically and testing via omnibus likelihood ratio tests, as well as stratified models by treatment arm and testing for treatment arm interactions for analyses of enzalutamide clearance. All point estimates are reported along with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
Statistical significance was determined at a Bonferroni‐corrected alpha level of 0.05 unless otherwise stated, applying two‐sided hypotheses where appropriate. All statistical analyses were performed in R v4.2.2 (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria).
Data collection and statistical analyses were conducted by the Alliance Statistics and Data Management Center. Data quality was ensured by review of data by the Alliance Statistics and Data Management Center and by the study chairperson following Alliance policies. All analyses were based on the study database frozen on 9/30/2021.
2.7
Single‐
SNP
Association Analyses
Single‐variant association analyses with clearance estimates were performed using the software PLINK 1.9 under an additive genetic model. Analyses were performed on all observed and imputed variants with an MAF > 0.05. Analyses were restricted to participants of European ancestry per the description above.
Association analyses were performed in a two‐tiered fashion based on the list of 10 pre‐specified candidate pharmacogenes in Figure
S1
. Targeted analyses were restricted to individual SNPs in or near (within 100 kb of the gene start or end site) the candidate pharmacogenes and were tested for association with drug clearance for both abiraterone and enzalutamide. To account for multiple testing in the presence of linkage disequilibrium, the effective number of independent SNPs was estimated using Gao's simple approach [
23
], performed separately for each outcome (Table
S2
). This yielded Bonferroni‐adjusted alpha levels of ~1e‐04 for both analyses. Genome‐wide analyses extending to all imputed and observed sites were performed and interpreted for significance using the conventional alpha = 5E‐08 threshold, with
p
< 1e‐05 treated as suggestive findings. All associations were adjusted for relevant covariates as described above and in Table
S3
. Regional association plots were generated using LocusZoom [
24
], while statistical fine‐mapping at significant loci was performed with SuSiE [
25
] to investigate association architecture and possible secondary associations.
2.8
Variant Annotation and Interpretation
Individual variant associations were annotated based on rsID and uploaded to FUMA v1.6.1 [
26
] for annotation and summarization. The predicted functional impact of SNPs was assessed using RegulomeDB V2.1 [
27
]. Evidence of SNP regulatory effects on liver and adrenal gland gene expression and liver protein expression was based on respective quantitative trait loci (eQTL and pQTL) association results from the Gene‐Tissue Expression (GTEx) portal [
28
] on 01/08/2025 and from 1508 proteins that were quantified in 287 human liver samples described in He et al. [
29
].

Study Highlights
What is the current knowledge on the topic?
○
Use of abiraterone or enzalutamide is a standard of care treatment for metastatic prostate cancer, but adverse side effects are common.
What question did this study address?
○
The study evaluated the relationship between genetic variants and oral clearance of abiraterone and enzalutamide.
What does this study add to our knowledge?
○
The study identified genetic variants within
SULT2A1
that are significantly associated with lower oral clearance of abiraterone.
How might this change clinical pharmacology or translational science?
○
This study is the first to show that inter‐individual variation in abiraterone exposure is governed in part by genetic variability in
SULT2A1
, which encodes a metabolizing enzyme present in adrenal tissues where abiraterone is known to exert its pharmacodynamic effect.
1
Introduction
The Alliance for Clinical Trials in Oncology A031201 phase III clinical trial for patients with metastatic castration‐resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) compared the clinical outcomes of treatment with enzalutamide alone versus enzalutamide plus abiraterone acetate and prednisone (AAP) [
1
]. The trial was designed on the basis that the drugs target androgen receptor signaling by different mechanisms and that the mechanism of action each drug may counteract the potential resistance pathways of the other. The combination arm of the trial did demonstrate statistically significant longer radiographic progression‐free survival (rPFS, median rPFS 24.3 months vs. 21.3 months in the enzalutamide alone arm, HR = 0.86,
p
= 0.02) [
1
]. However, the difference in overall survival was not statistically significant, and given the increased toxicities that were observed in the combination arm, the clinical benefit of combination therapy was limited.
Alliance A031201 was designed with parallel correlative studies, enabling pharmacokinetic (PK) and genome‐wide association studies (GWAS). PK studies in the published clinical trial identified a significant drug–drug interaction, in that participants receiving enzalutamide plus AAP had a two‐ to three‐fold higher metabolic clearance rate of abiraterone relative to the historical clearance rate of abiraterone monotherapy. The higher clearance of abiraterone was postulated as a reason for blunting the clinical impact of the combination arm, but it was also noted that the effect did not prevent the combination from having more side effects than enzalutamide alone [
1
].
Given that abiraterone and enzalutamide are both standard of care treatments for mCRPC [
2
,
3
,
4
,
5
], identification of the pharmacokinetic predictors of each drug may provide valuable information to determine the most appropriate drug and dosing to achieve minimal toxicity on an individual basis. For example, enzalutamide is known to have a greater potential as a perpetrator for drug–drug interactions [
6
] as enzalutamide is a strong inducer of CYP3A4 and a moderate inducer of CYP2C19 and CYP2D6 [
7
,
8
]. On the other hand, abiraterone has fewer drug–drug interactions, but its absorption is poor and is affected by food intake, and greater interpatient variability in exposure is observed [
9
]. Pharmacogenetic studies of abiraterone and enzalutamide clearance may provide keys to improved treatment selection and dose reduction, but to date these studies have been limited to the investigation of known candidate genes.
Abiraterone is primarily metabolized by sulfotransferase family 2A member 1 (
SULT2A1
) [
10
] and is a minor substrate of CYP3A4 [
6
]. Early resequencing studies of the
SULT2A1
coding regions identified several polymorphisms that were significantly correlated with SULT2A1 activity in biochemical assays [
11
] demonstrating potential for genetic variants that may determine abiraterone clearance, but population‐based pharmacokinetic‐pharmacogenomic studies of abiraterone clearance in relation to this gene are lacking. Genetic association testing in 81 healthy Chinese recently reported association of polymorphisms in the drug transporter
SLCO2B1
(but not
CYP3A4
or
UGT1A4
) with pharmacokinetic variability of abiraterone and its metabolites under both fasted and fed conditions, but this study was unable to assess
SULT2A1
genetic variation [
12
].
Therefore, in the current study, we evaluated whether genome‐wide genetic variants or genetically defined metabolic phenotypes of enzalutamide and abiraterone can be identified and associated with the variability in inter‐individual drug clearance.

3
Results
3.1
Genetic Data
A total of 13/967 (1.3%) of participants with initial genotyping were excluded based on sample‐level QC: three removed due to low call rate < 98%; 2 samples removed due to inconsistency of X and Y chromosome genotyping and reported sex; and 8 samples removed due to low heterozygosity on individual chromosomes. Four percent of SNPs were removed with call rates < 98%. No individuals were estimated to be related based on kinship coefficients > 0.125 (i.e., first cousins). Genotype concordance was > 99% for all 16 duplicate pairs, and the Centre d'Etude du Polymorphisme Humain (CEPH) trios were well genotyped (call rate > 99%) and showed a low rate of Mendelian errors (< 0.01). Among the 954 QC‐passed participants, 783 (82.1%) corresponded to ADMIXTURE EUR > 0.80. All primary genetic association analyses were performed within the European ancestry subset defined by ADMIXTURE [
16
].
3.2
Participant Characteristics
Among the 1311 A031201 trial participants, QC‐passed genome‐wide genotyping and PK data were available for 853 (65%) participants, of whom
n
= 706 were of European ancestry (Table
1
, Figure
1
). Within this analysis cohort, 340 (48%) were assigned to the enzalutamide plus AAP arm and thus had abiraterone oral clearance estimates available. The median age was 71 years (IQR 66–78) and the median BMI was 30 (IQR 27–34).

3.3
Enzalutamide and Abiraterone Clearance
Enzalutamide clearance values were highly skewed and log‐transformed for analyses (Figure
S4
). Clearance estimates were statistically significantly higher in patients receiving combination treatment with abiraterone than in patients receiving single‐agent enzalutamide (median clearance 0.48 versus 0.46 L/h,
p
< 0.001). Age exhibited a curvilinear relationship with clearance (Figure
S5
), while higher BMI and higher BSA were significantly associated with higher clearance (Table
S3
). Given the strong positive correlation between BMI and BSA, final multivariable models included treatment arm, age, age
2
, and BSA.
Similarly, abiraterone clearance values demonstrated a highly skewed distribution, and log‐transformed values were used in all analyses (Figure
S2
). Association analyses of abiraterone clearance with clinical and demographic characteristics among EUR participants revealed a significant negatively correlated relationship with age (
β
= −0.015, 95% CI: [−0.028, −0.002],
p
= 0.023). Further examination of the age association indicated a quadratic relationship with log‐transformed clearance. No other clinical or demographic variables were strongly associated with abiraterone clearance, nor were any leading PCs (Table
S3
). Final multivariable association analyses were adjusted for age and age
2
.
3.4
Genetic Variation Associations With Enzalutamide and Abiraterone Oral Clearance
There was no significant association between primary pharmacogene CYP3A4 activity and enzalutamide oral clearance in unadjusted or adjusted models (Table
2
, Table
S4
). Increasing CYP2C19 metabolic phenotype was nominally associated with lower enzalutamide oral clearance under the additive activity model (β = −0.0275; 95% CI: [−0.0503, −0.0047];
p
= 0.018). However, this result was in the opposite direction of that expected by biology. Sensitivity analyses did not reveal any significant gene‐treatment interactions (data not shown).

4
Discussion
Through comprehensive and detailed pharmacokinetic‐pharmacogenomic analysis of enzalutamide and abiraterone treated patients in the Alliance A031201 study, we identified for the first time genetic associations of variants in
SULT2A1
with reduced abiraterone clearance, also corresponding to associations of the same alleles with lower
SULT2A1
gene and protein expression. As a known key steroid and drug metabolizing enzyme present in both the liver and the adrenal glands, these data provide important evidence that
SULT2A1
genetic variation governs abiraterone clinical exposure—information that could be useful to inform personalized dosing regimens for this critical prostate cancer therapy.
Abiraterone is known to be primarily cleared by hepatic metabolism to abiraterone sulphate by SULT2A1. In our analysis, multiple common variants (MAF = 0.15 in European ancestry) mapping to the
SULT2A1
5′ flanking region, 3′ flanking region, and to
SULT2A1
intron 3 were associated with lower abiraterone clearance. Statistical fine‐mapping suggested that the causal variants of abiraterone oral clearance map to the
SULT2A1
5′ flanking region. This region was supported by a proteome‐wide association study in human liver samples, and by a meta‐analysis of 14,846 individuals, which found genome‐wide association of the rs2637125‐A allele with lower plasma concentrations of the endogenous substrate of SULT2A1 dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) [
30
]. The same allele was also strongly associated with lower abiraterone oral clearance in Alliance A031201 participants, and lower SULT2A1 gene and protein expression. Exon sequencing studies have reported additional missense variants in
SULT2A1
common in individuals with African ancestry (rs11569681 Ala63Pro, rs11569680 Lys227Glu and rs11569679 Ala261Thr) that are associated with decreased SULT2A1 activity [
11
,
31
]. These variants should be additionally investigated for their relationship with abiraterone oral clearance in cohorts with ancestral diversity.
A recent study of 81 healthy Chinese subjects reported that
SLCO2B1
rs1077858 and other variants at this locus [
12
] were associated with increased abiraterone exposure (AUC
0‐t
and
C
max
). In contrast, our study did not find an association of abiraterone oral clearance with rs1077858, nearby variants, or with
SLCO2B1
transporter phenotype. This could be due to differences in abiraterone dosing (250 mg vs. 1000 mg) or populations (Asian vs. European) between the studies. Unfortunately, Hu et al. [
12
] did not investigate associations of
SULT2A1
. Additionally, neither study found genetic associations of abiraterone oral clearance with the metabolic activity of other relevant pharmacogenes including
CYP3A4
,
UGT1A4
, or
HSD3B1/2
.
Inter‐individual variability of abiraterone pharmacokinetics [
32
] has been attributed in part to food intake, because administration with a high‐fat meal considerably increases abiraterone systemic exposure [
33
,
34
,
35
,
36
]. Alliance A031201 participants were instructed to take abiraterone in the evening without food; therefore, the food effect should be minimal and was not evaluable. However, our study did identify other non‐genetic factors associated with abiraterone and enzalutamide oral clearance. Firstly, it demonstrated a small statistically significant decrease in the clearance of both enzalutamide and abiraterone acetate with increasing age. Earlier studies showed no effect of patient age on pharmacokinetic profiles of either drug [
9
,
32
,
37
], but the ABGENE PK study [
38
] observed significantly higher concentrations of abiraterone in patients > 75 years. We note here that specifically, SULT2A1 expression in liver (in our protein dataset) and a prior study of
SULT2A1
expression [
39
], was not correlated with age. Secondly, for enzalutamide oral clearance, our study demonstrated strong associations with small to moderate effect sizes of BMI and BSA, which differed from the current literature [
40
]. Thirdly, the clearance rate of enzalutamide was statistically significantly higher in the combination arm relative to enzalutamide alone, suggesting a drug–drug interaction. The small effect size diminishes clinical relevance, but we emphasize that this finding illustrates a strength of population PK analysis and was not reported in the primary clinical trial publication [
1
].
Recent PK studies of abiraterone demonstrate tentative associations with efficacy, but replication is required in larger samples. A study of 61 mCRPC patients found higher plasma abiraterone concentrations in patients who responded to abiraterone, and improved progression‐free survival [
41
]. Metabolites of abiraterone and DHEA, the endogenous substrate of SULT2A1, have also been associated with progression‐free survival [
42
], shorter time to progression [
43
], and abiraterone response at the time of progression [
44
]. Taken together with the genetic findings in
SULT2A1
, one might predict that carriers of
SULT2A1
alleles that reduce abiraterone oral clearance may also be associated with clinical outcome. Therefore, we believe that the current literature and our findings of genetic association with
SULT2A1
warrant PGx studies of these variants with clinical outcomes to determine whether PGx data can potentially better optimize abiraterone treatment. Similarly, our findings may also be informative for abiraterone toxicities, although the association of abiraterone toxicity with PK profiles in the literature is lacking, and the ABGENE PK study did not identify any associations with toxicity grades [
38
]. Finally, studies of enzalutamide PK to date have shown no association with efficacy or toxicity [
6
,
40
,
45
,
46
] although we note here that the study sample sizes were small, compromising the power of such findings. Our study did find a novel association (although not significant after Bonferroni adjustment) of the
CYP2C8
*3 allele with increased clearance of enzalutamide. A recent review of
CYP2C8
*3 which consists of two non‐synonymous SNPs, rs11572080 and rs10509681 [
47
], supports the notion of bidirectional substrate‐dependent activity of this variant [
48
], with increased activity for several substrates including pioglitazone, rosiglitazone, and repaglinide. Further investigation of the metabolic activity of
CYP2C8*3
for various substrates, including enzalutamide, may be informative for personalized dosing to enhance efficacy or reduce toxicity. The strengths of this study are the convergent evidence from pharmacokinetics, GWAS and targeted SNP approaches in mCRPC clinical trial participants, combined with gene and protein expression data, pointing to
SULT2A1
as a potentially important PGx variable for abiraterone treatment. Beta for each SNP effect on log transformed abiraterone clearance ranged from −0.363 to −0.457, such that when back transformed, the effect size corresponds to a proportional decrease in clearance of 30%–40% per additional alternative allele, although we caution that this is a preliminary estimate and confirmatory pharmacokinetic studies are needed. Weaknesses of the study include the fact that we did not include a replication sample, and did not study non‐European descent individuals in this primary analysis (due to sample size limitations in under‐represented groups). Similarly, sample size was low by conventional GWAS standards and limited the statistical power for discovery of genome‐wide single‐SNP associations, although the associations with
SULT2A1
approached genome‐wide statistical significance. Finally, our single SNP analyses of candidate genes were limited to variants within 100 kb of each gene such that associated regulatory variants > 100 kb could have been missed. Future directions are to examine genetic associations with treatment response, patient survival, and toxicities, particularly comparisons between carriers and non‐carriers of the SULT2A1 diminished clearance variants.
In summary, genetic variants that reduce expression of
SULT2A1
, the major metabolizer of abiraterone, reduce abiraterone oral clearance in Alliance A031201 participants. This is the first study to identify genetic variants at the
SULT2A1
locus that may be relevant to personalized abiraterone dosing to improve treatment outcomes.
